newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgaria government faces thorny reform path.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgaria government faces thorny reform path.

text.p: Bulgaria on Monday awaited final results from parliamentary elections with the Union of Democratic Forces, confident of a comfortable majority but faced with the task of pushing through painful economic reforms.
The UDF won 52 percent of the votes cast in Saturday's election. Most of the results have now been counted.

The first task of the new parliament and government, due to be formed by mid-May, will be to pass a 1997 budget and package of banking laws needed to implement tough measures agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
Bulgaria's interim cabinet signed a $657 million funding deal with the IMF earlier this month, which included the introduction of a restrictive monetary mechanism known as currency board.

Freeing prices and trade rules and providing an investor-friendly legal climate to aid a swift transition to a market economy are also crucial steps which the new government must take, as is privatisation.
"Bulgarians have so far gone through severe hardships without the benefit of reform," said U.S. economist and president of Novecon trading firm Richard Rahn.
"What the government needs to do is to put together a comprehensive package within the next couple of weeks and get it passed through parliament as a single unit," Rahn added.
He urged the government to cut taxes and overhaul the complicated taxation system to encourage people to pay taxes instead of evading them.

Delayed reforms by eight revolving-door governments in seven years, corruption and asset stripping of major state-owned companies by a handful of shady businesses, have led to a grave economic crisis.
Galloping inflation -- measured at more than 2,000 percent annually in March -- has slashed incomes, devoured savings and sent the national currency into free fall earlier this year.

"The new leaders should realise that the price of reform has already been paid and now is the time to carry out the reform itself. If not, the costs will be dire," director of the Institute for Market Economics Krassen Stanchev told Reuters.

Under the currency board system due to be introduced in June, the amount of levs in circulation must be matched precisely by the amount of foreign exchange reserves. Central bank lending to the government and banks is banned.
Parliament has yet to vote whether to peg the lev to the dollar or the mark.

The central bank will be transformed into an issue department, a banking department to be used as a lender of last resort by local commercial banks only when there is danger of systemic risk, and a bank supervision department.
Major reform targets set out in Bulgaria's agreement with the IMF include:
-- Speeding up privatisation. Within two years Bulgaria pledged to privatise all commercial enterprises and half of the utilities.
-- Privatise all state mills by end-1997 to encourage competition in the market. Privatise or eliminate 26 state trading companies which monopolise all trade by end-1997.
-- Privatise six state owned banks by mid 1998.
-- Amend bank bankruptcy law to speed up closures of 11 banks now placed in receivership.
-- Strengthen bank supervision.
-- Revise existing ban on foreign land ownership, which restricts foreign investment in agriculture.
-- Promote an active agricultural land market. Set up a legal and institutional framework for mortgaging land.
-- Abolish price controls and trade barriers for farm goods. Eliminate the system of profit margins on agricultural products by end-May 1997.
-- Removal of price controls and trade barriers on fuels.
-- Utilities should generate sufficient revenues to cover their operating and financial expenditures. Prices will need to be adjusted monthly.

-- Set up a social safety net to compensate the poor and the jobless. Unemployment is already running at some 14.5 percent and with the closures of loss-making state firms is expected to rise by some 160,000 this year.
